prompt: Of the returns policy's 884 words, how many does all-MiniLM-L6-v2 read?
Appending "Returns are never accepted." to the end of the policy left its vector unchanged. Why?

choices.text: The vector was cached from the first run
choices.why: Nothing is cached; both were computed in the same call.

choices.text: It was past the 256th piece
choices.why: Right: same input after truncation, similarity 1.0000.

choices.text: The model ignores negative sentences
choices.why: A negative sentence inside the limit would be read like any other.

choices.text: The sentence is too short to matter in an average
choices.why: Any word inside the limit moves the average a little; this one was outside.

prompt: Which of these is NOT one of the lesson's reasons to cut documents into chunks?
hint: Three reasons: a limit, an average, a budget.

choices.text: The embedding model reads only so many pieces
choices.why: That is the first reason.

choices.text: Vector databases refuse long texts
choices.why: Right: the database stores whatever it is given; the limits are the model's and the prompt's.

choices.text: Whatever is retrieved is paid for in the prompt
choices.why: That is the third.

choices.text: A long text's vector is about none of its topics in particular
choices.why: That is the second.

prompt: Where did the 60-word chunks of the returns policy start and end?

choices.text: At full stops, rounded to the nearest sentence
choices.why: No rounding: the cut lands where the count says.

choices.text: In the middle of sentences
choices.why: Right: every boundary in the capture is mid-sentence.

choices.text: At the `## ` headings
choices.why: That is the sections strategy.

choices.text: At the start of each paragraph
choices.why: fixed counts words and ignores paragraphs.

prompt: A team indexes transcripts of support calls, with no punctuation or paragraphs. Which strategy does the lesson suggest?
hint: There is no structure to follow.

choices.text: Cutting at the headings
choices.why: A transcript has no headings.

choices.text: Structured chunks, packed by paragraph
choices.why: There are no paragraphs to pack.

choices.text: One chunk per call, whatever its length
choices.why: Long calls would be truncated after the model's limit.

choices.text: Fixed-size chunks with 10 to 20 per cent overlap
choices.why: Right, or semantic cuts with a size limit; both work without structure.

prompt: Fixed-size chunking guarantees every chunk is under the embedding model's ___, as long as the size is set below it.
With 60-word chunks and 15 words of overlap, how many chunks did the returns policy make?
hint: The first line of the second run.

prompt: With overlap, chunk 4 still ended in the middle of "Select the books you are". Why did that no longer matter?

choices.text: Chunk 5 holds the sentence whole
choices.why: Right: a second copy of the text, with no cut in it.

choices.text: Chunk 4 was merged with chunk 5
choices.why: Nothing merges; both chunks are in the index.

choices.text: The cut was moved to the end of the sentence
choices.why: The cut stayed where the count put it.

choices.text: Sentences in numbered lists are kept whole
choices.why: fixed knows nothing about lists.

prompt: Overlap raised the found count from 19 to 22 of 26. What new problem does it bring to the prompt?

choices.text: Some sentences arrive twice
choices.why: Right; lesson 12 removes such duplicates.

choices.text: Chunks exceed the embedding model's limit
choices.why: They are still 60 words.

choices.text: The citations point at the wrong document
choices.why: Both chunks come from the same document.

choices.text: The prompt loses the question
choices.why: Nothing about overlap touches the question.

prompt: What does the heading path give a chunk that its own text lacks?
hint: The damaged-books chunk says "a book" and "14 days".

choices.text: An embedding that ignores the 256-piece limit
choices.why: Nothing escapes the limit.

choices.text: What it is about and where it came from
choices.why: Right: the chunk becomes self-describing.

choices.text: A guarantee that it is the current version
choices.why: A path names a section, not a status; lesson 5 stores status separately.

choices.text: A smaller size, so it fits more easily in the prompt
choices.why: The path adds a few words; it does not shrink anything.

prompt: Why does structured() keep the steps of How to start a return and "Returns are free" in one chunk?

choices.text: It looks for the word "free" and keeps it with the steps
choices.why: It knows nothing about words; only paragraphs and sections.

choices.text: They fit under 120 words inside one section
choices.why: Right: paragraphs are packed until the next one would pass the size.

choices.text: Numbered lists are never split
choices.why: A list is paragraphs to it; this one happened to fit.

choices.text: The semantic similarity between them is high
choices.why: structured() embeds nothing.

prompt: A document is one 900-word paragraph with no headings. What does structured(text, 120) produce?
hint: A paragraph is never split, and sections need a heading.

choices.text: One 900-word chunk, mostly unread by the model
choices.why: Close, but with no `## ` heading there is no section at all to cut.

choices.text: A chunk per sentence
choices.why: It does not split sentences.

choices.text: Nothing
choices.why: Right: sections() returns nothing without a `## ` heading, so no chunk is made. The recursive version handles this.

choices.text: Eight chunks of about 120 words
choices.why: That is fixed-size behaviour; structured never splits a paragraph.

prompt: Put the separators of a recursive splitter in the order it tries them.
Where does semantic chunking cut?

choices.text: At each heading
choices.why: It strips the headings and never looks at them.

choices.text: Every fixed number of sentences
choices.why: No count is involved.

choices.text: Where two neighbouring sentences are least alike
choices.why: Right: the lowest quarter of similarities, here.

choices.text: Where the question's similarity is highest
choices.why: Cutting happens before any question exists.

prompt: How many words was the longest chunk semantic chunking made from the returns policy?
Why were the four numbered steps of starting a return split across three semantic chunks?
hint: Each step is a different action.

choices.text: Different actions read as different topics
choices.why: Right: they belong together and do not resemble each other.

choices.text: The steps are longer than 256 pieces
choices.why: Each step is a sentence or two.

choices.text: The list markers broke the sentence splitter
choices.why: The lookbehind keeps markers attached; chunks 6 to 8 start with them.

choices.text: The quantile was set too high
choices.why: A lower quantile cuts less everywhere; the steps would still be the weak links.

prompt: How many of the 26 answerable questions did structured 120-word chunks find?
Fixed 240-word chunks found 24 of 26. Why does the lesson call them the worst trade in the table?

choices.text: Too many tokens per question
choices.why: Right: 531 more tokens on every question, for one answer fewer than structured 120.

choices.text: They found the answers by accident
choices.why: Nothing in the table points to luck; the cost is the argument.

choices.text: They exceed the embedding model's limit
choices.why: Close to it, but 194 words average; the cost is the argument.

choices.text: They make citations impossible
choices.why: A big chunk can still be cited.

prompt: A colleague sees structured 120 at 25/26 and sections at 25/26, and structured 60 at 24/26, and concludes structured 60 is worse. What does the lesson say?
hint: How much is one question worth here?

choices.text: One question in 26 is too small a difference to decide on
choices.why: Right, and structured 60 also has the cheapest context of the three.

choices.text: The test set is wrong and should be rewritten
choices.why: It is small, not wrong; act on the large differences.

choices.text: Agree: any difference in found count decides
choices.why: With 26 questions, one is four points; too small to decide on.

choices.text: Structured 60 is better because it has more chunks
choices.why: More chunks is a cost, not a quality.

prompt: Match each strategy to what compare.py measured for it.
What does small-to-big retrieval search, and what does it return?

choices.text: Searches sections, returns sentences
choices.why: The other way round.

choices.text: Searches small units, returns their parents
choices.why: Right: precise search, enough context.

choices.text: Searches whole documents, returns a summary
choices.why: No summaries are involved.

choices.text: Searches and returns the same chunks
choices.why: That is ordinary retrieval.

prompt: Why did small-to-big not beat plain section search on this corpus?

choices.text: It returned fewer tokens
choices.why: It returned slightly more, 272 against 260.

choices.text: The sections are short and about one thing, so their vectors are already precise
choices.why: Right; it earns its place on long, mixed sections.

choices.text: Parents were looked up wrongly
choices.why: The lookup is by stored number and works.

choices.text: Sentences are too short to embed
choices.why: They embed fine; 319 of them were searched.

prompt: LlamaIndex's name for returning the matched sentence with a few sentences either side is a sentence ___.
hint: Like a frame around the hit.

prompt: What does the lesson say to keep after choosing a chunking strategy?

choices.text: The numbers that justified the choice
choices.why: Right, so it can be made again when the corpus changes.

choices.text: The embedding model's weights
choices.why: Those are the provider's, not a chunking decision.

choices.text: Only the winning strategy's code, deleting the rest
choices.why: The comparison is what lets the decision be revisited.

choices.text: A copy of every chunk ever made
choices.why: The index keeps the current chunks; old ones are not the point.

prompt: Which of these did the lesson measure as true on this corpus? Choose all that apply.
hint: Check each against compare.py and truncation.py.

choices.text: Overlap improved fixed 60-word chunks
choices.why: Yes: 19 to 22.

choices.text: Text after the 256th piece does not change the vector
choices.why: Yes: similarity 1.0000 with a sentence appended.

choices.text: Semantic chunking found more than cutting at headings
choices.why: No: 20 against 25.

choices.text: Thirty-word chunks found the most answers
choices.why: No: the fewest, 15.

choices.text: Structured 60 had the cheapest context of those above 15
choices.why: Yes: 170 tokens for 24.
